column3: Exact parallel: a clear sign is called fabricated magic because it was not heard from the ancestors.
Links the focus's divided reception to hardened hearts and far-reaching schism, but not to inherited religion.
Counters inherited communal labels by directing attention to Abraham's non-associating religion.
Treats ancestral custom as the sole frame for dismissing a message, though without the hearing claim.
Immediate opening: the oath by the Qur'an of remembrance introduces the warning that the opponents reject.
Creation and remembrance form only a remote contrast with the focus's inherited-religion objection.
Near-verbatim parallel: leaders reject a messenger as unheard of among their forefathers.
Immediate continuation: they contest why the remembrance was sent to him and remain in doubt about it.
Presents Abraham's religion as a followed path, qualifying the focus's appeal to inherited religion.
Those who hear recitation dismiss it as tales of the ancients, closely matching the focus's rejection formula.
Doubt is shared, but the barrier and deferred desire do not clarify the ancestral-hearing claim.
Opponents seek to force messengers back into their own religion, exposing inherited religion as coercive allegiance.
Shows a different response to a heard report: believers refuse to turn it into a baseless accusation.
Immediate parallel: the arrival of a warner is met with the labels magician and liar.
The creation-based self-exaltation is a different objection within the surah.
Identifies Abraham's religion as a chosen orientation rather than an unquestioned inherited convention.
Immediate context: the rejecting group is characterized by pride and schism before voicing its objections.
The bare statement of human creation does not develop the focus's reception or tradition theme.
Shares only the demonstrative expression, without a meaningful thematic connection.
Acknowledgment under punishment is only a remote counterpart to present rejection of warning.
Divine hearing in reassurance does not address communal refusal to hear a message.
Another elite group reduces a messenger to an ordinary human, a related defensive dismissal.
Immediate continuation: the objection centers on the unprecedented demand for one God.
Divine hearing and sight are not the disputed social hearing in the focus.
Combines claimed hearing with disobedience and verbal distortion, a related pattern of corrupt reception.
A later paradise description has no material relation to the objection in 38:7.
Divine hearing accompanies creation and resurrection, not rejection of a transmitted message.
Creation and the latter arising are outside the focus's dispute over religious inheritance.
Pharaoh's defensive labels of magician or madman echo the focus's move from warning to discrediting speech.
The call to examine creation is not connected to the claim of fabrication.
Hearing coupled with disobedience provides a counterpattern to receptive hearing of revelation.
Immediate continuation: the leaders organize perseverance in their gods and frame the call as a plot.
Communal approval is made conditional on following another group's religion, paralleling inherited religious pressure.
Joseph explicitly leaves a disbelieving people's religion, challenging the authority of inherited affiliation.
Job's affliction is unrelated to the warning and reception sequence.
Connects right religion with following Abraham rather than preserving an inherited communal formula.
Disbelievers question what God intends by a sign, a related move from disclosure to dismissive speech.
The domestic dispute has only the abstract term schism in common.
Creation in truth is too remote from the focus's accusation of invention.
The latter-life warning does not illuminate the reception of the new message.
Immediate surah summary: every prior group denied messengers, placing the focus's objection in that pattern.
The demand to affirm creation is a broad denial theme, not a reception parallel.
The creator question does not bear on the claim that revelation is fabricated.
Directly portrays opponents preventing others from hearing the Qur'an through disruptive speech.
Defines the straight religion through Abraham and non-association, correcting the focus's inherited-religion appeal.
Commands adherence to Abraham's religion, an alternative criterion to inherited communal practice.
The horse scene does not contribute to the focus's dispute.
Future hearing and sight do not explain the present rejection of revelation.
Distinguishes Solomon from a charge of magic while showing how harmful teachings circulate under false attribution.
A warner from among the people is received as something astonishing, closely echoing the opening dispute in Sad.
The descent from the Creator supplies only a distant revelation context.
The debt-writing instruction is unrelated to the candidate focus.
A later description of subjected devils has no connection to the objection sequence.
Exclusion from hearing gives a limited contrast to the focus's claim that the message was never heard.
Near-repeated pattern: ancestral repetition is dismissed as tales of the former peoples.
Remembrance and insight are relevant only as a broad positive counterpart to rejected remembrance.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are given capacities whose misuse contextualizes the focus's failed reception.
Near-repeated pattern: an inherited promise is dismissed as tales of the ancients.
Immediate historical warning: earlier generations cried out too late after the same rejecting posture.
Monotheism and creation address a related object of denial but not the focus's inherited-hearing logic.
Directly recasts the revelation as merely human speech, matching the focus's accusation of fabrication.
A revealed book becomes disputed and leaves people in troubling doubt, a broader reception parallel.
Creation signs for understanding do not address the focus's polemical claim.
A later statement about heavenly dispute is not connected to the focus's public objection.
The punishment description is only a distant consequence within the surah.
Creation and guidance do not develop the contested hearing or religious inheritance theme.
The contrast of worldly play and the hereafter is too remote.
The oath by the glorious Qur'an parallels 38:1's Qur'anic opening and its ensuing hostile reception.
Divine hearing in a command to seek refuge is unrelated to communal refusal of revelation.
Answers demands around angelic descent with divine truth and judgment, a limited context for rejecting revelation.
The later mention of Abraham and his family does not clarify the focus's use of religion.
A contrasting reception: hearers recognize the Qur'an as wondrous rather than fabricated.
The formula of exclusive denial expresses a comparable refusal of a disputed future claim.
Warning by revelation meets those unable to hear the call, a broad counterpart to the focus's failed hearing.
Individual creation does not bear on the accusation made in 38:7.
Directly labels the message inherited magic, closely matching the focus's fabrication charge.
Immediate surah history of peoples who denied before them reinforces the focus's opposition pattern.
The invitation to inspect creation is not a close inter-ayah relation here.
Measured descent of all things is too general to explain the social rejection at issue.
Clear recited signs are immediately called obvious magic, a close parallel to the focus's denunciation.
The creation-grounded call to worship is only a distant monotheism parallel.
Contrasting response: hearing guidance leads to faith rather than calling it invented.
The later praise of mountains with David does not develop the objection sequence.
Creation in truth and repudiation of partners are broader than the focus's reception logic.
The opponents' formula, 'this is only clear magic,' directly parallels the focus's discrediting label.
David's distraction from remembrance is unrelated to the communal denial in 38:7.
The impotence of false gods is a broad monotheism argument, not a close reception link.
Divine possession of first and last has no material connection to the focus.
The expulsion of Iblis is a separate later scene in the surah.
Creation from nothing is not tied to the focus's accusation of invention.
They listen without comprehension and call the message tales of the ancients, closely matching both parts of the focus.
Contrasting reception: believers say they hear and obey when called to divine judgment.
Ignorance of the unseen and resurrection timing is unrelated to the inherited-religion objection.
Depicts listening that fails to become understanding, a broader counterpart to the focus's rejection.
The trial and plea of Moses' delegates do not clarify the focus's claim.
Iblis's refusal based on Adam's material is a distinct objection pattern.
The life-and-killing command is unrelated despite its mention of clear messengers.
Creation without fatigue does not develop the focus's hearing or fabrication language.
Bearing the burdens of those led astray is only a distant consequence of misleading speech.
The collapse of alleged intercessions is unrelated to the immediate reception dispute.
Direct ancestral-religion parallel: they refuse revelation in favor of following what they found their fathers following.
Direct parallel: the appeal to God's revelation is rejected as unnecessary beside ancestral practice.
Wrong action is defended by appeal to what the fathers practiced, a related inherited-authority claim.
The people reject exclusive worship because it would require leaving what their fathers worshipped.
The appeal to ancestral association explains inherited error as a continuing communal defense.
Direct fabrication challenge: opponents say the recited Qur'an has been forged.
Moses and Aaron are resisted for turning people away from the way of their fathers.
Directly records the charge that the Qur'an has been fabricated.
Salih is rejected because his call would make the people abandon what their fathers worshipped.
Their worship is explicitly described as no more than what their fathers worshipped before.
Revelation is dismissed as tales of the former peoples.
A change in revelation is answered with the accusation, 'You are only a forger.'
Opponents cycle through dreams, invention, and poetry to discredit the revelation.
Abraham's people justify idolatry by saying they found their fathers devoted to it.
The inherited-worship rationale is stated without qualification: they found their fathers worshipping idols.
Abraham answers that both the people and their fathers are in manifest error, directly contesting ancestral authority.
A messenger is accused of inventing a lie about God, a close parallel to the focus's fabrication charge.
The disbelievers call the Qur'an a falsehood that Muhammad has fabricated.
The Qur'an is dismissed as tales of the ancients written down for him.
Idolaters defend their worship because they found their fathers doing it.
Directly answers the recurring charge that the revealed Book has been fabricated.
The messenger is accused of inventing a lie about God or of being possessed.
Clear verses are called an invented lie while the messenger is accused of turning people from their fathers' worship.
Messengers are reduced to ordinary humans whose supposed revelation the opponents refuse to accept.
They reject the messenger as a mad poet because his call would require abandoning their gods.
People are said to have found their fathers astray and rushed after their tracks.
Directly frames and rebuts the accusation that he has invented a lie about God.
They claim to have found their fathers upon a religious way and to be guided by their traces.
Generalizes the exact pattern: every warner meets people following their fathers' religious way.
The inherited way is retained even when a warner brings guidance better than what the fathers followed.
When the truth comes, it is called magic and rejected.
The truth is dismissed as an old falsehood when the opponents refuse to accept it.
Directly records the charge, 'He has fabricated it,' against the recitation.
A seen sign is dismissed as continuing magic, a related discrediting reflex.
Recited signs are called tales of the ancients.
The same formula, 'tales of the ancients,' is used to deny the recited signs.
Associators extend their defense to themselves and their fathers, treating inherited association as a settled excuse.
Associators invoke divine will to defend practices shared with their fathers, preserving inherited religious error.
A false claim about God is said to lack knowledge in both the speakers and their fathers.
Abraham exposes worship of what cannot benefit or harm, directly confronting the ancestral idol practice in the preceding exchange.
The resurrection promise is challenged through the fate of the speakers and their fathers, immediately before its dismissal as ancient tales.
When called to revelation, they answer that following what their fathers followed is sufficient.
Resurrection is resisted by invoking the prior condition of the speakers and their forefathers as bones and dust.
The opponents explicitly extend their resurrection objection to their first forefathers.
Clear signs meet the demand to bring back the fathers, making ancestral precedent the condition of belief.
A son rejects resurrection by citing vanished generations and calls the promise tales of the ancients.
The resurrection objection includes the speakers and their forefathers after they become dust and bones.
